title: Reply: the self-witness objection is a sophism — even a complete written word would face the same charge
source_text: XXIX. Respondeo argumentum istud, utut speciosum sit, merum esse sophisma, quod facile ostendi potest. Quamvis enim Pontificii negent totum Dei verbum Scriptura sacra contineri, negare tamen non possunt quin Deus saltem potuerit integrum suum verbum scripto tradere, & Apostolis praecipere ut scriptis mandarent omnia quae ipsis revelata erant, & quae Ecclesiam scire opus erat: Et quin, hoc casu posito, vera esset nostra thesis, nempe, Scripturam sacram esse sufficientem & perfectam fidei regulam; & nihil posse tanquam ad fidem & salutem necessarium urgeri, quod ipsa non contineretur. Et tamen, hac hypothesi facta, liceret eodem modo argumentari, & probare omnia ad fidem pertinentia non posse sufficienter haberi ex Scriptura sacra: nam hoc ipsum, quod talis Scriptura divinitus inspirata esset, & constaret his atque illis libris, res esset maxime pertinens ad fidem: Et tamen non posset istud ex Scriptura probari: quoniam, scilicet, nihil probat seipsum, nec potest aliquis credere testimonio alicujus Scripturae se divinam asserentis, quin prius persuasus sit illam esse divinam. Unde concluderetur necessarium esse verbum quoddam non scriptum praeter illam Scripturam, quod testimonium illi perhiberet, & quo nostra fides de Scriptura istiusmodi niteretur. Quae tamen conclusio, ex hypothesi facta, manifesto falsa esset, adeoque necesse est argumentum allatum falsum & sophisticum esse, quandoquidem ex eo falsum concludi potest.
pass_a_gloss: I answer that that argument, however specious it is, is a mere sophism, which can easily be shown. For although the Pontiffs deny that the whole word of God is contained in sacred Scripture, yet they cannot deny that God at least could have handed over His whole word in writing, and commanded the Apostles to commit to writings all things which had been revealed to them, and which the Church needed to know: And that, this case being posited, our thesis would be true, namely, that sacred Scripture is a sufficient and perfect rule of faith; and that nothing can be urged as necessary to faith and salvation which it did not contain. And yet, this hypothesis being made, one might argue in the same way, and prove that all things pertaining to faith cannot be sufficiently had from sacred Scripture: for this very thing, that such Scripture would be divinely inspired, and would consist of these and those books, would be a matter most pertaining to faith: And yet that could not be proved from Scripture: because, namely, nothing proves itself, nor can anyone believe the testimony of some Scripture asserting itself divine unless he is first persuaded that it is divine. Whence it would be concluded that some unwritten word besides that Scripture is necessary, which would bear testimony to it, and on which our faith concerning such Scripture would rest. Which conclusion, however, on the hypothesis made, would be manifestly false, and therefore the argument brought must be false and sophistic, since from it something false can be concluded.
pass_b_english: Answer: however showy, the argument is a mere sophism.
Rome admits God could have put His whole word in writing and ordered the Apostles to write all the Church must know — and then our thesis would be true.
Yet the same objection would still run: that this complete Scripture is inspired and these are its books is itself a faith-matter Scripture cannot prove, since nothing proves itself.
That would again demand an unwritten witness — a conclusion false under the hypothesis — so the argument that yields it is sophistic.

choices.english: something false can be concluded from it
